title: Act III, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Brutus speaks to the plebeians in prose: he loved Caesar, but loved Rome more; Caesar was ambitious, so he killed him. The crowd cheers and even shouts to make Brutus Caesar. Brutus leaves Antony to speak. Antony, in verse, repeats that 'Brutus is an honourable man' until the phrase turns to irony; recalls Caesar refusing the crown; weeps; shows the torn, bloody mantle; and finally reads Caesar's will, which leaves every citizen seventy-five drachmas and his private gardens. The crowd riots to burn the conspirators' houses. Antony hears Octavius is in Rome and that Brutus and Cassius have fled.

context.history: Roman funeral orations (laudationes) praised the dead in public. Rhetoric, the study of persuasion, was central to Roman and Elizabethan education; students practiced ethos, pathos and logos.

significance: This is the play's great study in persuasion. Brutus appeals to reason and his own honor; Antony uses repetition, irony, props, delay and emotion. The crowd's swing shows how rhetoric can move a republic toward violence.
